paragraphs: This paper studies poisoning attacks against models trained or fine-tuned on incoming data. In this setting, an attacker can adapt poisoned batches to the model’s current state. That differs from poisoning a fixed offline dataset, where malicious examples must be prepared before training and may reach the model in an unpredictable order.

The proposed strategy adds an accumulative preparation phase before a poisoned trigger batch. During preparation, the attack preserves accuracy while making the model more vulnerable to the later trigger. Its central idea is that the effects of malicious training data can build up without immediately appearing as worse predictive performance.

Experiments mimicking online and federated learning on MNIST and CIFAR-10 show a substantial accuracy drop after a single update using the trigger batch. These results demonstrate that a relatively straightforward strategy can amplify poisoning damage in the studied settings. They also show why accuracy during the preparation phase does not reveal the full effect: the visible degradation arrives only after the model encounters the trigger.
neurips-2021-accumulative-poisoning-atta.tldr: An accumulative poisoning strategy preserves accuracy during preparation while amplifying the damage caused by a later poisoned training batch.

paragraphs: Image super-resolution networks reconstruct higher-resolution images, but even lightweight architectures can contain redundant parameters. This paper targets that remaining redundancy through pruning. The challenge is that removing filters from residual blocks requires coordination across layers, making ordinary filter pruning difficult to apply directly to these networks.

The proposed aligned structured sparsity learning method introduces weight normalization and applies L2 regularization to its scale parameters to encourage sparsity. It also adds a penalty that aligns the locations selected for pruning across different layers. This penalty minimizes a norm of a soft-mask Gram matrix, giving the learning process an explicit way to coordinate which parts of the network become removable.

The authors use this strategy to train a super-resolution network called ASSLN. In their comparisons, it has fewer parameters and lower computational requirements than state-of-the-art methods while delivering better quantitative and visual results than recent lightweight networks. The contribution connects compression with reconstruction quality: coordinated pruning can remove redundancy while supporting strong image reconstruction in the evaluated models.
neurips-2021-aligned-structured-sparsity.tldr: Coordinating sparsity across layers produces a smaller, cheaper super-resolution network with improved results in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: This paper examines how to learn sparse Granger-causal relationships from events recorded over time. It focuses on Hawkes processes, which model temporal event data. Sparsity matters because the intended explanation should identify a limited set of relevant relationships, making individual events easier to analyze.

The authors identify a mathematical problem in most existing sparse causal-learning algorithms for Hawkes processes: their maximum-likelihood estimation has a singularity. Consequently, an apparently sparse result can arise from numerical behavior rather than a well-defined sparse solution. This distinction matters because an algorithm returning a small set of relationships does not, by itself, establish that its mathematical formulation supports that result.

The proposed framework uses cardinality regularization, which directly concerns the number of relationships retained, to provide a well-defined sparse learning problem and remedy the identified pathology. The authors apply it to instance-wise causal event analysis and validate it in power-grid and cloud-data-center management use cases. The contribution is therefore both foundational and practical: it repairs the basis for sparse estimation and uses that formulation to analyze particular events.
neurips-2021-cardinality-regularized-haw.tldr: Cardinality regularization gives sparse Hawkes-process causal learning a well-defined formulation that avoids an identified estimation singularity.

paragraphs: CAiDA adapts knowledge from several source domains to an unlabeled target domain using only pretrained source models. The original source data are unavailable during adaptation. This addresses a practical obstacle to combining knowledge across domains when retaining or accessing the underlying datasets is undesirable because of privacy or storage concerns.

The method first estimates how much transferable knowledge each source contributes. It then constructs a group of confident target examples that act as anchors. Less-confident examples receive pseudo labels through their semantically nearest confident anchors, providing training signals without source data or target labels. A further consistency loss aligns soft confusion matrices across domains to preserve relationships among classes.

These components address complementary needs: selecting useful source knowledge, assigning target labels, and maintaining class structure during adaptation. The paper provides theoretical analysis of the benefit of multiple sources and a learning bound supporting their use. Experiments on several representative datasets report stronger performance for CAiDA. The stated evidence supports combining source models through explicit contribution estimates and target-domain anchors in the studied adaptation setting.
neurips-2021-confident-anchor-induced-mu.tldr: CAiDA combines pretrained source models and confident target examples to adapt to an unlabeled domain without accessing source data.

paragraphs: Robust submodular partitioning divides items into blocks while maximizing the score of the weakest block. This objective encourages diversity throughout the partition, rather than allowing a few strong blocks to compensate for poor ones. The paper extends the problem by imposing additional requirements on every block, including size, matroid, and knapsack constraints.

Such constraints make the formulation useful for data allocation. For distributed training, the objective can encourage informative blocks, while extra rules can require equal numbers of examples from each class. The authors develop two algorithm families: Min-Block Greedy methods with an approximation bound of order 1/m, and Round-Robin Greedy methods with a constant approximation bound, where m is the number of blocks.

The guarantees continue to hold under various studied constraints. Although Round-Robin Greedy normally has only weakly polynomial running time, combining the two families produces a strongly polynomial algorithm while preserving the approximation guarantee. An application to a real-world machine-learning partitioning problem also gives good results. The main contribution is a way to combine balanced block quality, allocation requirements, and provable computational guarantees.
neurips-2021-constrained-robust-submodul.tldr: Greedy algorithms partition items into diverse, constrained blocks with approximation guarantees, and their combination improves the running-time guarantee.

paragraphs: This paper develops convergence theory for directly learning linear controllers that account for risk or disturbances. Its policy-gradient methods can be implemented without direct derivative access by sampling system trajectories. The goal is to connect this sampling-based form of controller learning with guarantees about both reaching a solution and the amount of data required.

The analysis covers two finite-horizon settings: linear exponential quadratic Gaussian control and linear-quadratic disturbance attenuation. For these problems, the authors establish global convergence and sample-complexity results. Their analysis also yields a sample-complexity guarantee for globally convergent policy-gradient methods in zero-sum linear-quadratic dynamic games, whose optimization is nonconvex in one participant’s choices and nonconcave in the other’s.

A central feature is what the authors call implicit regularization: the controller preserves a certain level of robustness or risk sensitivity during learning. That property concerns intermediate controllers, not just the final solution, which makes it relevant to safety-critical control. The guarantees apply to the specified linear control and game settings, providing a theoretical foundation for trajectory-based policy optimization within those problems.
neurips-2021-derivative-free-policy-opti.tldr: Trajectory-based policy optimization receives global convergence and sample-complexity guarantees while preserving some robustness or risk sensitivity during learning.

paragraphs: This paper studies principal component analysis when data are randomly distributed across several computing nodes. The associated leading-eigenvector problem is formulated on a sphere, reflecting the constraint that the sought direction has unit length. The question is how to solve this distributed problem efficiently while limiting the information that nodes must exchange.

The authors propose a quantized version of Riemannian gradient descent. Riemannian optimization handles the spherical geometry, while quantization reduces the precision used to communicate information. Combining these ideas makes communication part of the algorithm’s design rather than treating distributed computation as ordinary optimization with unrestricted messages between nodes.

The paper proves convergence with high probability under the required spherical-convexity properties. It also bounds the total number of transmitted bits for common initialization schemes and examines how those bounds depend on dimension. These results connect the algorithm’s ability to reach a solution with its communication cost. The stated guarantee depends on the geometric conditions and the random distribution of data, rather than covering every possible distributed arrangement.
neurips-2021-distributed-principal-compo.tldr: Quantized Riemannian gradient descent solves distributed PCA with conditional high-probability convergence and bounds on communication in bits.

paragraphs: Generalized zero-shot learning recognizes both previously seen categories and new categories described through semantic information such as attributes. A central difficulty is confusion between these groups. This paper addresses that domain-shift problem by improving two properties together: how well visual representations transfer to new categories and how clearly they distinguish categories.

The Dual Progressive Prototype Network maintains prototypes for attributes and categories. Attribute prototypes guide a repeated process of finding relevant image regions and refining the prototypes themselves. This progressively improves the correspondence between an attribute and its visual location, supporting alignment between semantic descriptions and image features.

Alongside attribute localization, category prototypes are projected into multiple spaces to progressively separate visual representations from different categories. The two prototype systems are learned jointly, so transferability and category separation develop within one framework. Experiments on four benchmarks show that DPPN alleviates the studied domain-shift problem. The findings support treating accurate attribute localization and category discrimination as complementary parts of recognizing unfamiliar categories.
neurips-2021-dual-progressive-prototype-.tldr: DPPN jointly refines attribute locations and category separation to reduce confusion between seen and unseen categories.

paragraphs: Estimating a new treatment’s long-term effect is difficult when only older treatments have long-term follow-up. This paper combines two complementary datasets: historical observations with long-term outcomes and observations of novel treatments with only short-term outcomes. Its surrogate-based approach uses short-term information to connect the evidence available in these two settings.

The method extends earlier surrogate approaches to allow continuous treatments and treatment policies that are correlated across time. These extensions broaden the kinds of treatment sequences the analysis can accommodate. Under a Markovian assumption on both the data and the observational policy, the authors establish consistency and root-n asymptotic normality for their estimates.

Consistency describes convergence toward the target effect as data increase, while the asymptotic result characterizes estimation uncertainty at the root-n scale. These are conditional statistical guarantees tied to the stated Markovian assumption. The authors evaluate the method on a semi-synthetic customer-incentive dataset from a major corporation and discuss deployment challenges. The contribution is a framework for using historical follow-up to inform estimates for treatments whose own long-term outcomes are not yet observed.
neurips-2021-estimating-the-long-term-ef.tldr: A surrogate-based estimator combines historical long-term outcomes with new-treatment short-term data, with statistical guarantees under a Markovian assumption.

paragraphs: G-PATE aims to generate useful synthetic data while providing differential privacy for the generator. It builds on the PATE framework and adversarial generation, using an ensemble of teacher discriminators to train a student generator. The key challenge is to pass useful learning signals from the teachers without exposing sensitive information through those signals.

The paper introduces private gradient aggregation to protect all information flowing from teacher discriminators to the student. Because gradients can be high-dimensional, the method combines random projection with gradient discretization to make aggregation manageable. These mechanisms address the practical difficulty of applying privacy protection to the large vectors used in generator training.

The authors prove a differential-privacy guarantee for G-PATE and report improved use of privacy budgets relative to existing approaches. Their experiments show stronger results than prior work, including high-utility, high-dimensional generated images under budgets with epsilon at most one. The stated advance is the combination of a formal privacy guarantee and empirical data utility in this demanding setting, supported by a training design that controls teacher-to-student information transfer.
neurips-2021-g-pate-scalable-differentia.tldr: G-PATE privately aggregates teacher gradients to train useful high-dimensional data generators under limited differential-privacy budgets.

paragraphs: An agent operating among several possible targets must understand which one an instruction refers to. Without prior target knowledge, learning this distinction can require many samples and generalize poorly. This paper introduces an additional learning signal intended to help reinforcement-learning agents distinguish goals through semantic understanding.

The proposed goal-aware cross-entropy loss uses automatically labeled goal states in a self-supervised way alongside reinforcement learning. Building on that loss, the authors design goal-discriminative attention networks. These networks use information relevant to the goal to focus on the instruction, connecting target discrimination with the attention used to guide behavior.

The methods are evaluated on visual navigation and robot-arm manipulation in environments containing multiple targets. The reported results improve task success, sample efficiency, and generalization relative to state-of-the-art methods. Qualitative analyses also indicate clearer attention to the supplied instruction. Together, the findings support teaching an agent to distinguish goals explicitly as part of learning how to act, with benefits demonstrated across both navigation and manipulation tasks.
neurips-2021-goal-aware-cross-entropy-fo.tldr: A self-supervised goal-discrimination loss helps attention-based reinforcement-learning agents follow instructions more successfully and efficiently.

paragraphs: Recovering sparse data often involves optimization with an L1 objective, as in Basis Pursuit. These problems can be difficult to solve at large scale because the objective is nonsmooth. Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares, or IRLS, is widely used for such recovery and performs well numerically, but previous convergence theory did not provide a global rate.

This paper proves a global linear convergence rate for a variant of IRLS. Here, linear convergence means that the error contracts geometrically as iterations proceed. The guarantee begins immediately from any initialization, provided the measurements satisfy the usual null space property. That condition is central to the claim: the result is not an unconditional guarantee for arbitrary measurement systems.

Numerical experiments support the theory and show that the rate captures the correct dependence on problem dimension. The result therefore strengthens an eventual-convergence statement into a description of how quickly error decreases throughout the run. The authors also anticipate implications for other IRLS applications, including low-rank matrix recovery, presenting that connection as a direction for further insight.
neurips-2021-iteratively-reweighted-leas.tldr: An IRLS variant has global linear convergence from any initialization when measurements satisfy the null space property.

paragraphs: Generating speech from lip movements is ambiguous because similar visible mouth patterns can correspond to different speech sounds. VCA-GAN addresses this by combining local lip information with broader visual context. Local features supply the immediate visual evidence, while context helps clarify cases in which that evidence alone does not determine the sound.

The generator learns a mapping from visible speech units to phonemes. A visual-context attention module builds global representations from local features and uses audio-visual attention to provide context appropriate to the generator’s coarse speech representation. This context enters intermediate generator layers, allowing it to influence speech synthesis as the output is developed.

The method also introduces synchronization learning through a contrastive objective, guiding generated speech to align with the input lip movements. Experiments report improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods and effective synthesis in a multiple-speaker setting, which earlier work had scarcely addressed. The approach combines three complementary requirements: interpreting local mouth shapes, resolving ambiguity through context, and keeping the resulting speech synchronized with the video.
neurips-2021-lip-to-speech-synthesis-wit.tldr: VCA-GAN combines local lip features, global visual context, and synchronization learning to improve speech generation from lip movements.

paragraphs: Structured probabilistic models represent distributions over combinations such as state sequences or grammatical structures. Their hidden representations can become expensive as the number of states increases. The paper highlights quadratic scaling for Hidden Markov Models and cubic scaling for Probabilistic Context-Free Grammars as obstacles to using larger latent spaces.

The proposed approach expresses the central inference operation as a matrix-vector product and imposes a low-rank constraint. Rank becomes a control over the balance between expressive capacity and computational cost. A lower-rank representation reduces the work and memory required by the operation, making this a shared strategy for a broad class of structured models.

Experiments apply the method to neural parameterizations for language, polyphonic music, unsupervised grammar induction, and video modeling. At large state-space sizes, the reported models match standard-model accuracy while providing practical speedups. These results show that the expressivity-speed tradeoff can be favorable in the evaluated tasks: constraining the inference representation can retain useful modeling accuracy while making large structured models more manageable.
neurips-2021-low-rank-constraints-for-fa.tldr: Low-rank constraints reduce structured-model inference costs while matching standard-model accuracy in the reported large-state-space experiments.

paragraphs: MetaAvatar reconstructs animatable clothed humans from monocular depth images. The difficult part is producing realistic clothing deformation under new poses while accommodating different bodies and garments. Existing approaches commonly require complete meshes or dense scans and expensive optimization for each subject or clothing type.

The method represents an avatar with a neural signed distance field, whose parameters are predicted by a pose-conditioned hypernetwork. Changing the pose therefore changes the represented clothed shape. Meta-learning supplies an initialization that incorporates experience across body shapes and clothing types, allowing the hypernetwork to adapt more quickly than a model trained from scratch.

The reported qualitative and quantitative comparisons favor MetaAvatar over state-of-the-art approaches that require complete mesh inputs, while MetaAvatar uses depth frames and runs orders of magnitude faster. The authors also demonstrate realistic dynamic clothing deformation from as few as eight monocular depth frames. The central finding is that a learned initialization can make sparse observations sufficient for the demonstrated avatar reconstructions while retaining pose-dependent control.
neurips-2021-metaavatar-learning-animata.tldr: MetaAvatar uses a meta-learned, pose-conditioned hypernetwork to create animatable clothed avatars from as few as eight depth frames.

paragraphs: Newton-style optimization uses curvature information, but constructing the Hessian at every iteration can be expensive. Randomized sketching approximates that information using a smaller computation. Dense Gaussian sketches offer attractive theoretical behavior, yet their computational cost creates tension between inexpensive sketching and fast optimization convergence.

Newton-LESS uses leverage-score-sparsified embeddings to make the sketch much sparser. The aim is to reduce the cost of constructing the approximation while retaining the convergence behavior associated with Gaussian sketches. For a large class of functions, the authors prove nearly the same problem-independent local convergence rate as with Gaussian embeddings.

This analysis yields a new state-of-the-art convergence result for an iterative least-squares solver. The paper also extends LESS embeddings to uniformly sparsified random-sign matrices, which admit efficient implementations and perform well in numerical experiments. The significance lies in the combination of cheaper sketching and strong convergence guarantees. The theorem described in the abstract is local and applies to a specified function class, so its scope concerns convergence in that analyzed regime.
neurips-2021-newton-less-sparsification-.tldr: Newton-LESS makes Hessian sketching cheaper while retaining nearly Gaussian-sketch local convergence rates for a large class of functions.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust optimization trains models to account for distribution shift, but its objective can be harder to optimize than an ordinary training loss. This paper studies the problem for general smooth nonconvex losses, seeking guarantees without the strong loss assumptions used in much previous theory.

The authors exploit the structure of the robust objective even when that objective is nonconvex, nonsmooth, and subject to unbounded gradient noise. They prove that mini-batch normalized gradient descent with momentum reaches an epsilon first-order stationary point using O(epsilon^-4) gradient evaluations. This is a finite-computation guarantee for approximate stationarity, rather than a claim of reaching a global optimum.

The paper also considers conditional value-at-risk, introducing a penalized objective based on a smoothed version of that criterion and obtaining a similar convergence guarantee. Experiments across several tasks report consistent acceleration from the proposed algorithm. Together, the theory and evaluations support an optimization method tailored to the structure of robust objectives, extending convergence analysis to settings with several simultaneous sources of difficulty.
neurips-2021-non-convex-distributionally.tldr: Normalized gradient descent with momentum has a finite gradient-complexity guarantee for approximate stationarity in challenging nonconvex DRO problems.

paragraphs: Two-stage recommenders first use fast nominators to select candidates and then apply a slower, more accurate ranker. This architecture scales recommendation to large item pools. The paper asks whether understanding each component independently is enough to explain the quality of the complete system.

Using synthetic and real-world data, the authors show that interactions between nominators and the ranker substantially affect performance. A generalization lower bound further establishes that training nominators independently can produce performance comparable to uniformly random recommendations. This is a possible failure of independent training, rather than a claim that all independently trained systems perform randomly.

The authors find that carefully assigning item pools to different nominators alleviates these problems. Because manually finding a good allocation is difficult, they learn the allocation using a Mixture-of-Experts approach. This significantly improves precision and recall at K in their evaluations. The findings make candidate-pool allocation part of the learning problem and show why the quality of a two-stage system depends on how its components work together.
neurips-2021-on-component-interactions-i.tldr: Learning which item pools nominators handle improves two-stage recommendations by addressing harmful interactions with the ranker.

paragraphs: This paper studies a foundational question in adversarial robustness: under what conditions does an optimal classifier actually exist? Bayes optimality identifies the best achievable classification rule for the relevant statistical objective. In the adversarial setting, that objective must account for the adversarial changes against which the classifier is meant to be robust.

The authors provide general sufficient conditions guaranteeing the existence of an adversarial Bayes-optimal classifier. The qualification matters: satisfying those conditions ensures existence, but the abstract does not assert that they are necessary. The result establishes that an optimal rule is attained under the stated conditions, giving later theoretical work a well-defined object to study.

The authors identify surrogate losses and their consistency as a possible use of this existence result. Such work concerns how an alternative training objective relates to the desired robust classification objective. Establishing that an adversarial optimum exists can support that analysis. The contribution is therefore a mathematical foundation for studying robust learning objectives, with its proposed value for subsequent consistency research expressed as a possibility.
neurips-2021-on-the-existence-of-the-adv.tldr: The paper gives sufficient conditions for an adversarial Bayes-optimal classifier to exist, supporting possible future analysis of surrogate-loss consistency.

paragraphs: Online knapsack requires making allocation choices as items arrive, before the entire input is known. This paper asks how much help predictions can provide when they contain very limited information. Its predictions specify only lower and upper bounds on the number of items at each value, rather than describing the complete future sequence.

For any fixed prediction of this form, the authors systematically derive algorithms achieving the best possible competitive ratio. That ratio measures worst-case performance relative to an optimal solution with advance knowledge. The result therefore connects the strength of an online guarantee to the particular frequency information supplied, rather than requiring a detailed forecast.

The paper extends its results to generalized one-way trading and two-stage online knapsack. Across these formulations, the central finding is that coarse predictions can still improve provable online performance. The optimality claim is tied to each fixed prediction and the studied setting. This makes the contribution useful for understanding the value of partial information: even interval bounds on frequencies can support stronger decisions.
neurips-2021-online-knapsack-with-freque.tldr: Bounds on item frequencies suffice to derive online knapsack algorithms with the best possible competitive ratio for each fixed prediction.

paragraphs: Multi-head attention lets a sequence model gather information from different parts of its input. When one model serves several languages or domains, sharing those heads can transfer useful knowledge, but it can also cause interference. This paper finds that sharing attention without selection is suboptimal for generalization across the studied languages and domains.

The authors propose strategies that automatically learn which attention heads should be shared and which should specialize. This places the sharing decision inside the learning process. The approach aims to preserve common capabilities while giving different languages or domains attention capacity suited to their particular requirements.

Evaluations cover speech recognition, text translation, and speech-to-text translation, with consistent gains for the tested models. In speech-to-text translation, the reported average improvement is 2.0 BLEU across 13 multilingual translation directions and 2.0 BLEU across three domains in the multi-domain setting. These findings support selective attention sharing as a practical way to balance transfer and specialization, with the numerical gains describing the evaluated settings rather than every language or domain.
neurips-2021-pay-better-attention-to-att.tldr: Learning which attention heads to share or specialize improves multilingual and multi-domain sequence modeling in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows can model probability distributions and energies, but physical applications also need smooth derivatives to compute forces. Molecular coordinates introduce another complication: angles and bond-related coordinates occupy spaces with periodic and bounded structure. This paper develops smooth flow transformations suited to compact intervals and hypertori, addressing both differentiability and the geometry of those spaces.

The transformations use mixtures whose inverses are computed numerically through root finding. That inversion procedure had prevented bidirectional flow training. The authors apply the inverse function theorem to show that parameter gradients and forces associated with an inverse can be calculated from forward evaluations, making the necessary derivative information accessible.

The paper demonstrates two uses of the resulting smooth flows: training through force matching against simulation data and serving as potentials in molecular dynamics simulations. These applications require more than approximating distribution values accurately; they also depend on usable energy derivatives. The contribution joins smooth transformations on the relevant coordinate spaces with a way to differentiate their numerically obtained inverses.
neurips-2021-smooth-normalizing-flows-e5.tldr: Smooth mixture flows support force-based training and molecular dynamics by enabling derivatives through numerically computed inverse transformations.

paragraphs: Many logistic-bandit models describe a binary response, such as clicking or not clicking. This paper studies decisions with several possible responses, each carrying its own revenue. A multinomial-logit model assigns outcome probabilities according to the learner’s action and unknown outcome-specific parameters, and the learner seeks to maximize expected revenue.

The proposed MNL-UCB algorithm uses upper confidence bounds to guide its choices while learning those parameters. The formulation accommodates K+1 outcomes, including the no-click outcome. This allows the decision problem to preserve distinctions among responses instead of reducing all feedback to a single binary event.

The authors prove a regret bound of order dK times the square root of T, up to logarithmic factors, where d is the parameter dimension and T the number of rounds. The bound has limited dependence on problem-specific constants that could otherwise become arbitrarily large and weaken the guarantee. Numerical simulations corroborate the analysis. The contribution extends confidence-based bandit learning to multiple revenue-bearing outcomes with a more informative theoretical performance bound.
neurips-2021-ucb-based-algorithms-for-mu.tldr: MNL-UCB handles multiple response outcomes with a regret guarantee that limits dependence on potentially large problem-specific constants.

paragraphs: The lottery ticket hypothesis motivates studying why a properly pruned neural network can generalize better than its original dense version. This paper analyzes that question through the geometry of the training objective and the number of samples needed to reach zero generalization error. Its theoretical setting is a neural network with one hidden layer.

Within that setting, pruning enlarges the convex region around a desirable model with guaranteed generalization. For training by stochastic gradient descent or its accelerated form, the required sample count is proportional to the number of retained hidden-layer weights. These results connect the network’s sparse structure to both the surrounding optimization landscape and its data requirements.

With a fixed number of samples, the analysis also gives faster convergence to the desired model for the pruned network than for the original network. Experiments explore implications for pruning networks with multiple layers. The distinction in scope matters: the formal results concern the one-hidden-layer setting, while the deeper-network evidence is experimental. Together, they provide a theoretical explanation and broader empirical support for benefits associated with winning tickets.
neurips-2021-why-lottery-ticket-wins-a-t.tldr: A one-hidden-layer analysis links pruning to favorable optimization geometry, lower sample requirements, and faster convergence.

paragraphs: Word meanings can evolve over both short and long periods. Many temporal word-representation methods train separate embeddings for predefined time groups and then align them. Word2Fun instead learns an explicit function of time for each word, representing semantic evolution as a continuous process within a unified representation.

This design reduces storage complexity from O(TVD) to O(kVD), where T is the number of time groups, V the vocabulary size, D the representation dimension, and k a small constant relative to T. The reduction comes from storing a compact temporal function rather than a separate representation for every time group.

The paper also studies a polynomial instance and invokes the Weierstrass approximation theorem to support its approximation capability for word-evolution functions under that theorem’s conditions. Evaluation covers time-aware word clustering, temporal analogy, and semantic-change detection. The contribution combines a compact way to represent change with an explicit temporal model. Its approximation argument concerns representational capability, while the task evaluations assess the effectiveness of learning and using those representations.
neurips-2021-word2fun-modelling-words-as.tldr: Word2Fun models each word as an explicit function of time, compactly representing semantic change across short and long periods.
